profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:40:30.234+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
Fengchì Biānjí
Hòu Xué Tiān Tāi
Emperor Wǔ, having rendered meritorious service to Liáng,
believed his surname originated from Chén,
and was promoted from Duke of Wúxīng Commandery to Duke of Chén;
upon receiving the mandate,
the state was thus named Chén.
Emperor Gāozǔ Wǔ
First Year of Yǒngdìng (Dīngchǒu, 557)
In this year, in the tenth month, he received the abdication,
and first changed the era name to Yǒngdìng.
Before the tenth month,
it was still the second year of Tàipíng of Liáng.
1 Spring,
first month,
Xīnchǒu,
the Duke of Zhōu ascended the throne as Heavenly King,
his personal name was Jué,
courtesy name Tuóluóní,
the third son of Yǔwén Tài.
Yǔwén assisted in governance,
admiring and emulating the Zhōu rituals,
Tài died,
Jué succeeded him,
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Zhōu;
upon receiving the mandate,
the state was named Zhōu.
He received the hundred officials in court at the Lù Gate;
the Lù Gate,
is the ancient Lù Gate.
Lù,
means great.
Yǔwén established the state,
generally imitating ancient institutions,
thus the outer court was called the Lù Gate.
Zhèng Xuán said: the outer gate is called the Gāo Gate,
the court gate is called the Yìng Gate,
inside there is the Lù Gate.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: the Ěryǎ states: the space between the gate and screen is called Zhù.
Guō said: where the ruler stands to observe the court.
Lǐ Xún said: the space between the two side rooms outside the main gate is called Zhù.
It is said that the Son of Heaven receives court in the court outside the Lù Gate,
standing at Zhù outside the gate,
waiting for the arrival of the feudal lords,
hence it is said he stands at Zhù.
However, where there is a screen outside the gate,
that is the Shù Sè Gate.
Ěryǎ states: the main gate is called the Yìng Gate.
It also states: the screen,
is called Shù.
Lǐ Xún said: often serving to conceal oneself at the gate,
named Shù.
Guō said: a small wall in the middle of the gate.
According to the annotations of Lǐ and Guō to infer the ritual texts,
the feudal lords' inner screen is inside the Lù Gate,
the Son of Heaven's outer screen is outside the Lù Gate,
and near the Yìng Gate.
Under the Zhōu system,
the Son of Heaven had three courts,
one inside the Lù Gate,
called the Yàn Court,
overseen by the Tàipú.
Thus the Tàipú states,
when the king observes the Yàn Court,
he rectifies his position.
The Wén Wáng Shìzǐ states: the ducal clan holds court in the inner court,
showing closeness.
This is where the king plans auspicious matters with his clansmen,
and where the king retires after the court of feudal lords and high officials.
The second is the court outside the Lù Gate,
called the Zhì Court,
overseen by the Sīshì.
Thus the Sīshì states,
he rectifies the positions for court ceremonies.
This is the position for daily court observation,
where the king and feudal lords engage in guest archery,
also the same as the Zhì Court.
The third is inside the Gāo Gate,
outside the Kù Gate,
called the Outer Court,
overseen by the Cháoshì.
This is the court for consulting the multitude.
Court,
pronounced Zhí Yáo Fān.
His deceased mother was honored as Empress Wén;
a great amnesty was declared.
Enfeoffed Emperor Gōng of Wèi as Duke of Sòng.
Taking the virtue of Wood to succeed Wèi's Water,
implementing the Xià calendar,
the color of garments honored black.
Implementing the Xià calendar,
using the Yín beginning.
The color of garments honored black,
following the Water phase.
Xià,
pronounced Hù Yǎ Fān.
Zhào Guì was appointed Grand Tutor,
Grand Steward Dúgū Xìn as Grand Guardian,
Grand Minister of Rites Duke of Zhōngshān Yǔwén Hù as Grand Marshal.
Later, Tàizǔ of Northern Zhōu initially controlled the area west of Hánguān,
official titles had not yet changed from the Wèi designations.
When the region was roughly stabilized,
he revised the statutes and regulations,
ordering the Imperial Secretary Lú Biàn to extensively study the Zhōu system,
establishing the Three Dukes and Three Solitaries,
as officials for discussing the Way;
then establishing the Six Ministers,
to divide and manage various affairs.
Emperor Mǐn received the abdication,
the Grand Marshal controlled the military,
Yǔwén Hù occupied this position,
to monopolize military authority.
2 An edict appointed Wáng Lín as Minister of Works, General of Agile Cavalry,
and appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Imperial Secretariat Wáng Tōng as Vice Director of the Left.
3. The Zhou emperor performed sacrifices at the Round Mound.
He claimed his ancestors descended from Shénnóng,
and thus paired Shénnóng with the two mounds.
The Yǔwén clan claimed their ancestors descended from Yándì.
Yándì was defeated by Huángdì,
and his descendants fled to the northern wilderness.
Later, there was one named Géwūtù,
who was valiant, martial, and full of strategy.
The Xiānbēi revered him as their lord.
A descendant named Pǔhuí,
while hunting, obtained three jade seals,
inscribed with the words
"Imperial Seal."
He considered this a heavenly mandate.
In their custom, the term for Son of Heaven was Yǔwén,
so they adopted it as their surname and state name.
The two mounds are
the Round Mound and the Square Mound.
Pǔhuí's son Mònà moved south from Yīnshān,
and first settled in Liáoxī.
His posthumous title was Marquis Xiàn.
His temple name was Tàizǔ.
On Guǐmǎo day,
sacrifices were performed at the Square Mound.
On Jiǎchén day,
the Great Altar of the Soil was sacrificed to.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* records: The Later Zhou modeled its statutes on the Zhōu of old,
and its sacrificial ceremonies
largely followed the *Yílǐ*.
The Director of Measures
was in charge of the regulations for constructing the altars.
The Round Mound had three tiers,
with a total height of one *zhàng* and two *chǐ*,
and a depth of two *zhàng*.
The upper diameter was six *zhàng*,
with twelve steps,
each level having twelve sections.
It was located in the suburb seven *lǐ* south of the capital.
The circular enclosure had a diameter of three hundred paces,
the inner enclosure half that.
The Square Mound had one tier,
with a lower height of one *zhàng*,
and a diameter of six *zhàng* and eight *chǐ*.
The upper height was five *chǐ*,
with a square side of four *zhàng*.
It had eight sides,
each with one stairway,
each stairway having ten steps,
each step one *chǐ* high.
The Square Mound was located in the suburb ten *lǐ* north of the capital,
with one tier and eight sides.
Its lower height was one *zhàng*,
with a square side of six *zhàng* and eight *chǐ*.
Its upper height was five *chǐ*,
with a square side of four *zhàng*.
Each of the eight sides had one stairway,
with steps one *chǐ* high.
Its enclosure had eight sides,
with a diameter of one hundred twenty paces,
the inner enclosure half that.
The southern suburb had a square altar five *lǐ* south of the capital,
with a height of one *zhàng* and two *chǐ*,
and a width of two *zhàng*.
Its enclosure was square, one hundred twenty paces per side,
the inner enclosure half that.
The altar of Shénzhōu
was one *zhàng* high,
with a square side of four *zhàng*.
It was located to the right of the Square Mound in the northern suburb,
and its enclosure was like that of the Square Mound.
Sacrifices at the Round Mound and the southern suburb
were both held on the first Xīn day of the first month.
The Ancestral Temple was on the right, and the Altars of Soil and Grain on the left.
The emperor personally sacrificed to the Altars of Soil and Grain,
with the Zhǒngzǎi performing the secondary offering,
and the Zōngbó the final offering.
At the end of the Wèi dynasty, bandits arose in great numbers,
and state funds were insufficient.
A tax of one coin per person was levied on those entering the city gates,
which was now abolished.
On Yǐsì day,
sacrifices were offered at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Following Zhèng Xuán's interpretation,
Tàizǔ and two Zhāo and two Mù temples were established as the five temples.
Those with particular virtue had separate, permanent temples,
which were not dismantled.
The *Wángzhì* records: The Son of Heaven has seven temples:
three Zhāo and three Mù,
together with the temple of Tàizǔ, making seven.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: This seven-temple system of the Zhōu
comprised Tàizǔ, the permanent temples of King Wén and King Wǔ, and four kin temples.
The *Juéyí Yàozhù* states: In the Zhāo-Mù arrangement,
the father faces south,
hence called Zhāo.
Zhāo
means bright.
The son faces north,
hence called Mù.
Mù
means obedient.
Lǐ Fú said: Zhāo
was originally pronounced according to its character,
but due to the Hàn taboo on the character Zhāo,
it was changed to Sháo.
Another explanation: Jìn Emperor Wén's personal name was Zhāo,
hence it was read as Sháo.
On Xīnhài day,
sacrifices were performed at the southern suburb.
On Rénzǐ day,
Empress Yuán was established.
The Empress
was Jìn'ān Princess, daughter of Wèi Emperor Wén.
4. Féng Xiǎn, the commander of the Southern Pacification city of Qí, requested to surrender to Zhōu.
Zhōu Pillar of State Yǔwén Guì sent Guō Yàn, Governor of Fēng Province from Tàiyuán, with troops to receive him.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* records: Huánggāng County of Yǒng'ān Commandery
was called Southern Pacification by Qí.
Also, the *Wèishū Zhì* records: In the early Tiānpíng era,
Southern Pacification Commandery was established,
belonging to Xiāng Province,
but later fell.
Based on geographical examination,
it should have been within the boundaries of Yè County, Yǐngchuān Commandery, as recorded in the *Wǔdài Zhì*.
Also, the *Wǔdài Zhì* records: Wǔdāng County of Xīyáng Commandery
formerly had Wǔdāng Commandery and Shǐpíng Commandery established,
later changed to Qíxīng Commandery.
Liáng established Xīng Province there,
later changed by Later Zhōu to Fēng Province,
and by Suí to Jūn Province.
Jiàng (to lead troops)
is pronounced *jíliàng*.
5. Tǔyùhún raided Zhōu,
attacking Liáng, Shàn, and Hé provinces.
Wǔwēi Commandery
was Liáng Province.
Xīpíng Commandery
was Shàn Province.
Fúhǎn Commandery
was Hé Province.
Tǔ
is pronounced with the entering tone of *tūn*.
Yù
is pronounced *yù*.
Shàn
is pronounced *shízhàn*.
In the third year of the Huángchū era of Wèi,
the office of Commander of Various Provincial Military Affairs was first established.
There was also the Commander of Military Affairs of the Capital and the Provinces,
whose responsibility was especially weighty.
Both the Southern and Northern Dynasties followed this.
Furthermore, for military campaigns, there were Commanders of Various Armies,
and Grand Commanders of the Left, Right, Front, Rear, and Center Armies.
Within, for palace guard duties,
there were Regular and Deputy Commanders, Scattered Commanders, Commander-Commandants, and Brigade Commanders.
Outside, in the provinces and commanderies,
there were City Defense Commanders and Tent Interior Commanders.
Although the title "Commander" was the same,
their positions and responsibilities varied greatly.
This Commander of Qín Province
likely commanded Hé, Wèi, Liáng, Shàn, and other provinces.
According to the Later Zhōu system of nine ranks of appointment,
Commander was an eight-rank appointment.
Those appointed as Pillar of State Grand General or Kāifǔ Yìtóng
were additionally given the authority of Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers and Grand Commander,
which was a nine-rank appointment.
His subordinates all voiced their opinions,
but Yì said:
"The art of attack and conquest
is not the strength of barbarian customs.
These raiders have come
merely to plunder the border pastures.
If they plunder and gain nothing,
they will likely leave of their own accord.
To weary our troops by going after them,
will certainly achieve nothing."
Yì had already thoroughly assessed the situation.
Liǎo
means clear.
Chāo (to plunder)
is pronounced *chǔjiāo*.
Chuǎi (to assess)
is pronounced *chūwěi*.
After several days,
news arrived,
and it indeed turned out as Yì had predicted.
6. Initially,
Emperor Shìzǔ of the Liang dynasty established Shǐxīng Commandery as Dōnghéng Province,
appointing Ōuyáng Wěi as its governor.
After some time,
he transferred Wěi to be the governor of Yǐng Province,
but Xiāo Bó detained Wěi and did not let him go.
Emperor Shìzǔ then appointed Wáng Lín to replace Bó as the governor of Guǎng Province.
Bó sent his general Sūn Dàng to oversee Guǎng Province,
and led all his troops to station at Shǐxīng to avoid Lín.
See scroll 165, third year of Chéngshèng reign of Emperor Yuán of Liang.
General,
pronounced as jìng;
same below.
Oversee,
pronounced as jiān.
Lead,
read as shuài.
Wěi did not go to pay respects,
instead closing his gates and defending himself.
Bó became angry,
sent troops to attack him,
and seized all his goods, wealth, horses, and weapons;
soon pardoned him,
restored him to his position,
and formed an alliance with him.
When Jiānglíng fell,
Wěi then served Bó.
In the second month,
on Gēngwǔ,
Bó raised troops in Guǎng Province,
sending Wěi and his generals Fù Tài and Xiāo Zī as the vanguard.
Zī
was Bó's nephew.
The governor of Nánjiāng Province, Yú Xiàoqīng, joined them with his troops.
Xiàoqīng occupied Xīnwú,
likely establishing Nánjiāng Province there,
and was appointed as its governor.
Examination of discrepancies: Diǎnlüè records
"governor of Nánkāng Province."
Here we follow the Book of Liang.
7. On Guǐyǒu,
the King of Zhōu performed the morning ceremony to the sun in the eastern suburbs;
on Wùyín,
he sacrificed at the Great Altar of the Land.
8. The Zhōu Dukes of Chǔ, Zhào Guì, and Wèi, Dúgū Xìn, were both originally equals to Tàizǔ.
Yǔwén Tài's temple name was Tàizǔ.
Yǔwén Hù was promoted from Duke of Zhōngshān to Duke of Jìn.
Guì plotted to kill Hù,
but Xìn stopped him;
the Kāifǔ Yìtóng Sānsī Yǔwén Shèng reported this.
On Dīnghài,
Guì came to court,
Hù arrested and killed him,
and dismissed Xìn from his post.
This is what is called when the ruler is young and the state is unstable,
and the great ministers are not yet loyal.
After killing Zhào Guì,
Hù's authority was established.
9. The General of the Imperial Guard, Xú Dù, went out from Dōngguān to invade Qí,
on Wùzǐ,
reached Héféi,
and burned three thousand Qí ships.
10. Ōuyáng Wěi and others set out from Nánkāng.
Wěi stationed at Kǔzhútān in Yùzhāng,
Fù Tài occupied the city of Zhíkǒu,
Yú Xiàoqīng sent his younger brother Xiàolài to guard the commandery city,
and went out himself to occupy Shítóu in Yùzhāng.
Commentary on the Water Classic: The Gàn River passes north of Yùzhāng Commandery,
on the western bank of the river is a stone slab,
called Shítóu,
a ferry crossing point.
Wāng Zǎo said: Crossing the river west from Yùzhāng,
there is a mountain standing tall,
emerging alongside the river,
which is Shítóu Island;
blocking the river and backing the city,
less than ten lǐ away,
is where Yīn Xiàn threw his letters.
Lài,
pronounced as mài.
Tán Fǎ,
agreed to join forces to defeat Wěi,
and said:
"If we succeed,
give me horses and weapons."
So he led his troops out,
and advanced together with Wěi.
When they reached the city of Fǎ,
Tánlǎng pretended to be defeated and fled,
Fǎ pursued him,
Wěi lost support and fled,
Tánlǎng took his horses and weapons,
and returned to Bāshān.
Zhōu Wényù's army lacked ships,
Yú Xiàoqīng had ships at Shàngláo,
Wényù sent the army commander Jiāo Sēngdù to raid them,
took them all and returned,
and still set up a stockade in Yùzhāng.
When the army ran out of food,
the generals wanted to retreat,
but Wényù did not allow it,
sending someone secretly to deliver a letter to Zhōu Dí,
proposing to become sworn brothers.
Dí was very pleased upon receiving the letter,
and promised to supply grain.
So Wényù sent the old and weak to go down the river in old ships,
burned the Yùzhāng stockade,
pretending to flee.
Xiàoqīng saw this,
was overjoyed,
and no longer took precautions.
Wényù took a shortcut and advanced quickly,
occupying Qiānsháo,
upstream from Qiānsháo were Ōuyáng Wěi and Xiāo Zī,
downstream were the camps of Fù Tài and Yú Xiàoqīng,
Wényù occupied the middle,
built a city and feasted his troops,
causing great alarm to Wěi and others.
Wěi retreated into Níxī,
Wényù sent General Yánwēi Zhōu Tiěhǔ and others to attack Wěi,
on Guǐsì,
captured him.
Wényù displayed his troops and armor in full array,
feasted with Wěi on a boat,
patrolled to the city of Zhíkǒu,
sent his general Dīng Fǎhóng to attack Tài,
and captured him.
Zī and Xiàoqīng retreated and fled.
11. On Jiǎwǔ,
Zhōu appointed Yú Jǐn as Grand Tutor,
the Grand Minister of Rites, Hóumòchén Chóng, as Grand Guardian,
Duke of Jìn, Yǔwén Hù, as Grand Steward,
Yú Jǐn and Hóumòchén Chóng, having ascended to the rank of duke,
if Yǔwén Hù were promoted in order to become Grand Steward,
he would actually be the chief minister of Zhōu.
Duke of Gāoyáng, Dáxī Wǔ, was appointed as Grand Minister of Justice.
12. The people of Zhōu killed Emperor Gōng of Wèi.
13. In the third month,
on Gēngzǐ,
Zhōu Wényù sent Ōuyáng Wěi and Fù Tài to Jiànkāng.
Chancellor Bàxiān had an old relationship with Wěi,
released him and treated him generously.
Bàxiān started his career in Lǐngnán,
hence his old relationship with Wěi.
14. Duke of Jìn of Zhōu, Yǔwén Hù, because Dúgū Xìn, Duke of Zhào, had a great reputation,
did not want to execute him publicly,
on Jǐyǒu,
forced him to commit suicide.
15. On Jiǎchén,
appointed the Minister of Works, Wáng Lín, as governor of Xiāng and Yǐng Provinces.
16. Marquis of Qǔjiāng, Bó, was in Nánkāng,
heard that Ōuyáng Wěi and others were defeated,
and the army was in panic and fear.
On Jiǎyín,
the governor of Dé Province, Chén Fǎwǔ,
Five Dynasties Records: Rìnán Commandery,
established Dé Province during the Liang dynasty.
killed him.
17. In summer,
the fourth month,
on Jǐmǎo,
cast the Four-Pillar coin,
one worth twenty.
At the end of the Liang dynasty, there were Two-Pillar coins and Goose-Eye coins,
which people used interchangeably,
their value was the same,
but the Two-Pillar was heavy,
the Goose-Eye was light.
Now they cast the Four-Pillar coin,
one worth twenty fine coins.
18. Qí sent an envoy to request peace.
19. On Rénwǔ,
the King of Zhōu visited Chénglíng;
the tomb of Zhōu Tàizǔ was called Chénglíng.
On Yǐyǒu,
he returned to the palace.
The state of Qí appointed the Tàishī Húlǜ Jīn as the Right Chancellor,
and the former Grand General Kězhūhún Dàoyuán as the Grand Tutor.
Kězhūhún Dàoyuán was formerly the Grand General of Cavalry.
Later, Qí established the offices of Tàishī, Tàifù, and Tàibǎo,
collectively known as the Three Masters,
which imitated the high offices of ancient times,
and could only be held by those with great merit and virtue.
Next in rank were the Grand Marshal and the Grand General,
known as the Two Grand Offices,
which jointly supervised military affairs.
Following them were the offices of Tàiwèi, Sītú, and Sīkōng,
forming the Three Dukes.
All were of the highest rank.
The two generals, Piāoqí and Chēqí, if elevated,
ranked below the Dukes of the Open States.
The Dukes of the Open States
were one rank below the highest.
The Secretary of the Board, Chángshān Wáng Yǎn, assumed the role of Sīkōng,
and the recorder of board affairs, Zhǎngguǎng Wáng Zhàn, became the Secretary of the Board.
The Right Attendant Yáng Yǐn was appointed as the Left Attendant,
and simultaneously given the status equivalent to the Three Masters.
The office of Right Attendant was abolished, and Cuī Xián was made Left Attendant,
with Shàngdǎng Wáng Huàn recording board affairs.
Since Gāohuān resided in Jìnyáng,
the governor of Bìngzhōu held the role of acting Head of the Board.
When the illustrious ancestor of Qí accepted the abdication of Wèi,
Bìngzhōu's acting authority became a merged province,
holding a position second to the Yè Province.
On the day Dīnghài,
King Zhōu made sacrifices at the Tàimiào.
On the day Rénchén,
the coinage of four-column currency was changed to a value of ten;
on the day Bǐngshēn,
the circulation of small coins was stopped.
Those prohibited,
they were completely forbidden from being used.
The small coins,
privately minted by commoners.
At that time, private coins were small and thin,
transactions were conducted by cart-loads of coins,
without individual counting.
Fù, here means restored or reversed;
below, fù also means the same.
The former Marquis of Qǔjiāng, Bó, and his officer Lán Ài attacked and killed Tán Shìyuǎn,
while the army leader Xiàhóu Míngchè killed Ài,
and brought Bó's head in surrender.
Bó's former secretary Lǐ Bǎocáng served Húiān Hóu Rèn, taking charge of Guǎngzhōu.
Rèn was also a scion of the Xiāo clan,
and was ennobled as Húiān Hóu.
Hé Chéngtiān's record states: "Yùlín County has a Húiān County."
There were two cities,
each occupying one,
with many ships and boats positioned,
stationed alongside the water.
The Chancellor Bàxiān dispatched General Hóu Āndū of the Southern Forces to assist Zhōu Wényù in attacking them.
On the day Wùxū,
Āndū secretly led his troops to set their ships ablaze at night,
Wényù led the navy, and Āndū led the infantry to advance in attack;
Xiāo Zī appeared in surrender,
while Xiào Qǐng fled back to Xīnwú,
Wényù and others returned their forces.
Chancellor Bàxiān, recognizing Ǒuyáng Wěi's fame in the southern regions,
reappointed Wěi as Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu,
"Héng"
refers to,
with the "East"
prefix.
According to the Wu Dynasty records: "Nánhǎi County includes Hánkōng County,"
instated by the Liáng as Héngzhōu.
Shǐxīng County,
established as Dōnghéngzhōu by the Liáng.
At this time, perhaps appointing Wěi to oversee Hánkōng.
Before arriving,
his son Hē had already conquered Shǐxīng,
once Wěi reached Língnán,
all counties surrendered,
thereby capturing Guǎngzhōu,
and the whole of Língnán was pacified.
This was the beginning of the Ǒuyáng family's control over Língnán for generations.
Zhōu Yítóng Sānsī Qí Guǐ said to Yùzhèng Zhōng Dàfū Xuē Shàn:
According to the Wu Dynasty records: "Yùzhèng Zhōng Dàfū,"
belonged to the Grand Steward,
having five ranks.
"The administration of the military and nation,
should belong to the Son of Heaven,
how could it still reside in powerful houses!"
Shàn reported this to Jìn Gōng Hù,
and Hù killed him,
appointing Shàn as the Sīmǎ of the Inner and Outer Palace.
The Inner and Outer Palace,
was the Command of Affairs over all military matters.
In May, on the day Wǔchén,
Yú Xiàoqǐng sent envoys to the Chancellor’s office requesting to surrender.
After Wáng Lín did not comply with the summons,
he greatly prepared ships and boats,
intending to attack Chén Bàxiān;
in June, on the day Wǔyín,
Bàxiān appointed Minister of the Open Court Hóu Āndū as the Commander of the Western Path,
and Zhōu Wényù as the Commander of the Southern Path,

(Lìng Xián) established ten cities,

Concern and questioning were directed at Yǎn.
Consolation,
expressed with the strength to act.
Yǎn constantly resided in the palace,
conducting affairs while seated in the Hánguāng Hall,
and all his uncles bowed to him.
The Retired Emperor occasionally traveled to Bìngzhōu,
as the Jìnyáng Palace was located in Bìngzhōu.
Each time he saw him off,
sometimes halfway,
sometimes only returning after reaching Jìnyáng.
Utensils, playthings, clothing, and ornaments
were all identical to those of the Qí sovereign,
and everything he required was supplied by the state.
Once, in the Southern Palace, he saw fresh ice and early plums,
the Qí sovereign at that time resided in the Southern Palace of Yè,
while Yǎn lived in the Northern Palace with the Retired Emperor and Empress Hú.
He angrily said:
"The Honored Elder Brother already has them,
why should I not have any!"
Yǎn often referred to the Qí sovereign as "Honored Elder Brother."
The subordinate officials and craftsmen were inevitably punished.
Yǎn's nature was resolute and decisive,
and he once said to the Retired Emperor:
"The Honored Elder Brother is timid,
how can he command his attendants!"
The Retired Emperor often praised his talent,
and had the intention to depose and establish him,
Empress Hú also encouraged this,
but eventually it was halted.
Although Yǎn and the Qí sovereign had established the distinction between sovereign and subject,
they often addressed each other as brothers,
and Yǎn also harbored the intention to seize the heir position.
The historian narrates this in detail,
to lay the groundwork for Yǎn's reliance on favor leading to disaster.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
23 Huá Jiǎo sent an envoy to entice Zhāng Zhāodá,
but Zhāodá captured him and sent him to Jiànkāng.
He also attempted to entice Chéng Língxǐ,
but Língxǐ executed him.
Huá Jiǎo, with Wǔzhōu situated at his heartland,
according to the Wǔdài Zhì,
the Wǔlíng Commandery,
was established as Wǔzhōu during Liáng.
Zǐ Lóng did not comply;
he sent troops to attack him,
but failed to conquer.
The Bāzhōu Prefect Dài Sēngshuò and others were all subordinate to Huá Jiǎo,
as Emperor Wén had ordered Huá Jiǎo to oversee four provinces including Xiāng and Bā.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì,
the Bālíng Commandery,
was established as Bāzhōu during Liáng.
Originally subordinate to Huá Jiǎo,
they thus served under him.
Xiāngzhōu shared its administrative seat with the Chángshā Commandery,
with the province governing the commandery,
hence it is said they were originally subordinate to Huá Jiǎo.
Shǒu,
read as shǒu.
Then, a special pardon was issued for Xiāng and Bā provinces.
In the ninth month,
on the yǐsì day,
all of Huá Jiǎo's family members were executed.
Liáng appointed Huá Jiǎo as Minister of Works,
and sent its Pillar of State Wáng Cāo to lead twenty thousand troops to assist him.
Zhōu's Quán Jǐngxuān commanded the naval forces,
Yuán Dìng commanded the land forces,
with Duke Wèi Zhí overseeing them,
and together with Huá Jiǎo, they advanced downstream.
Chún Yú Liàng stationed his army at Xiàkǒu,
Zhí stationed his at Lǔshān,
and sent Yuán Dìng with several thousand infantry and cavalry to besiege Yǐngzhōu.
Huá Jiǎo encamped at Báiluó,
according to the Shuǐjīng: the Jiāng River passes north of Xiàjuàn County in Chángshā,
where the Xiāng River flows from the south to join it.
The Jiāng River then flows east past Péngchéngkǒu,
then east past Rúshān north,
then east past Báiluóshān south.
Luó,
read as luó.
Juàn,
read as juàn.
Xú Dù and Yáng Wéntōng advanced via mountain paths to attack Xiāngzhōu,
the mountain paths,
were the same as the previously mentioned footpaths from Ānchéng and Yíyáng.
Huá Jiǎo, from Bālíng, along with the Zhōu and Liáng naval forces, sailed downstream with the wind,
their military momentum was very strong,
and they engaged in battle at Dùnkǒu.
Liàng and Míngchè recruited small vessels from their army,
offering generous rewards of gold and silver,
ordering them to go out first to face the large vessels of the Western army and withstand their catapults;
after the Western army's vessels had exhausted all their catapult shots,
then Liàng and others used large vessels to catapult them,
the Western army's vessels were all shattered,
and sank in the midstream.
Warships were equipped with catapult poles,
launched to strike enemy ships.
Jiàn,
read as jiàn.
They then set fire using the wind,
but shortly after, the wind shifted,
and they burned themselves,
leading to a great defeat for the Western army.
Huá Jiǎo and Dài Sēngshuò fled alone in a single boat,
passing Bālíng,
not daring to go ashore,
"fā",
likely should be
"dēng".
Duke Wèi Zhí also fled to Jiānglíng.
Yuán Dìng's isolated army,
with no path to advance or retreat,
cut bamboo to open a path,
fighting while retreating,
intending to head towards Bālíng.
Bālíng had already been occupied by Xú Dù and others,
Dù and others sent envoys pretending to form an alliance with him,
promising to allow him to return to his state;
Dìng believed them,
laid down his arms and approached Dù,
but Dù captured him,
and took all his troops prisoner,
Kǎo Yì says: the Chén Shū records
"capturing over ten thousand men,
and four thousand horses."
This is also likely exaggerated,
and is not adopted here.
Dìng died of anger and resentment.
Huá Jiǎo's partisans Cáo Qìng and over forty others were all executed.
Only Yuèyáng Prefect Zhāng Zhāoyù,
Zhāodá's younger brother,
Guìyáng Prefect Cáo Xuān,
a former minister of Emperor Gāozǔ,
Héngyáng Internal Historian Rǔyīn Rèn Zhōng,
who had once submitted secret memorials,
were all pardoned.
Wú Míngchè took advantage of the victory to attack Liáng's Hédōng,
and captured it.
Zhōu's Duke Wèi Zhí blamed Liáng's Pillar of State Yīn Liàng;
the Liáng sovereign knew it was not his fault,
but did not dare to oppose,
and thus executed him.
Since Zhōu and Chén had become hostile,
Zhōu's Miǎnzhōu Prefect Péi Kuān reported to the Xiāngzhōu Commander,
requesting to increase garrison troops,
and also to move the city to Yángtíshān to avoid flooding.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì: Zèngshān County in Miǎnyáng Commandery,
was established as Liáng'ān Commandery during Liáng,
renamed Wèi'ān Commandery by Western Wèi,
and Jiāngzhōu was established there,
in the third year of Emperor Fèi,
renamed Miǎnzhōu.
Zèngshān has Yángtáishān,
located thirty-five lǐ south of Hànchuān,
locally mispronounced as Yángtíshān.
Chéng Língxǐ's naval forces suddenly arrived at the city walls.
Heavy rain occurred,
causing a sudden flood,
Língxǐ brought large vessels close to the city and launched catapults,
shattering the towers and battlements,
attacking with arrows and stones day and night for over thirty days;
the Chén troops scaled the city walls,
but Kuān still led his men, holding short weapons to resist;
after another two days,
he was captured.
24 On the dīngsì day,
the Qí Retired Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
East of the mountains flooded,
causing famine,
according to Lǐ Bǎiyào's book: East of the mountains had a great flood,
and people starved.

the tenth month,
on the jiǎshēn day,

on the wùxū day, the first day of the month,

Zhōu's Duke Xǔmù Yǔwén Guì returned from the Tūjué,

Yǔwén Guì, along with Duke Chén Chún and others, went to the Tūjué to fetch a bride,
but the Tūjué detained them;
Guì, due to illness, was allowed to return first.
Jué,
read as jué.
Huán,
read as huán,

Zú,

Yè,

29 The Qí Retired Emperor returned to Yè.
30 In the twelfth month,
the mother of Zhōu's Duke Jìn Hù died,
an edict was issued for him to rise,
and ordered to resume his duties.
31. Zǔ Tǐng, the Secretary Supervisor of Qí,
was on friendly terms with the Deputy Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Liú Tì.
Tǐng sought the position of Chancellor,
so he drafted a memorial detailing the crimes of Zhào Yànshēn, Yuán Wényáo, and Hé Shìkāi,
and ordered Tì to submit it.
Tì did not dare to present it.
When Yànshēn and the others heard of this,
they went first to the Retired Emperor to explain themselves.
The Retired Emperor was furious.
He arrested Tǐng,
interrogated him,
and Tǐng then accused Shìkāi, Wényáo, Yànshēn, and others of forming factions, manipulating power, selling official posts, and accepting bribes in legal cases.
The Retired Emperor said:
"You are slandering me!"
Tǐng said:
"Your subject does not dare to slander Your Majesty for taking another man's daughter."
The Retired Emperor said:
"I took her in and raised her because she was starving."
Tǐng said:
"Why not open the granaries to provide relief,
instead of buying her into the rear palace?"
The Retired Emperor grew even angrier.
He struck Tǐng's mouth with the pommel of his sword,
rained down blows with whips and clubs,
and was about to beat him to death.
Tǐng cried out:
"Your Majesty, do not kill your subject!
Your subject can concoct golden elixirs for Your Majesty."
He was thus granted a slight reprieve.
Tǐng said:
"Your Majesty has a Fàn Zēng but cannot employ him."
(A saying of Emperor Gāo of Hàn.)
"You compare yourself to Fàn Zēng,
and take me for Xiàng Yǔ?"
Tǐng said:
"Xiàng Yǔ was a commoner,
who led a motley crowd,
and within five years established a hegemon's enterprise.
Your Majesty relies on the foundation laid by your father and elder brother,
and only thus have you reached this point.
Your subject believes Xiàng Yǔ should not be easily dismissed."
The Retired Emperor grew even more furious,
and ordered soil to be stuffed into his mouth.
Tǐng spat and spoke as he did so.
He was then given two hundred lashes,
assigned to the Armory Workshop,
and soon transferred to Guāngzhōu.
(Wǔdài Zhì: Dōnglái Commandery formerly established Guāngzhōu.)
The Assistant Administrator, Zhāng Fèngfú, said:
"'Prison' means an underground dungeon."
So he was placed in an underground dungeon,
shackles never leaving his body.
At night,
turnip seeds were used as candles,
and his eyes were damaged by the smoke,
causing him to go blind.
(Běncǎo states: Turnips are good for improving eyesight.
That Tǐng went blind because of them is likely because consuming the seeds improves eyesight,
but using them as candles,
the smoke damages the eyes and causes blindness.
Yǎnyì states: Turnips are what is commonly called mánjīng today.
They wither in summer,
and vegetable gardens replant them,
calling them jīmáocài.
Right in spring, after they are picked,
the seeds are collected for oil.
If this is accurate, then it is vegetable oil.
People in the southeast often use it for night lighting,
and it has never been known to damage eyes and cause blindness.)
Dù Yòu said: Wèi first established the Minister of the Five Arms,
meaning Central Arms, Outer Arms, Separate Arms, Capital Arms, and Cavalry Arms.
Jìn divided Central and Outer into Left and Right,
making seven sections in total compared to the old system,
but there was only the Minister of the Five Arms,
not the title Minister of the Seven Arms.
It was not until Later Wèi
that the Minister of the Seven Arms first appeared.
Now, various scholars' writings
sometimes say the Minister of the Seven Arms was established during the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
which is an error.)
It was beyond human reason,
and especially severe within the family.
At night,
he was killed by bandits,
who left behind their knife.
Upon examination,
it was the knife worn by his son, Shànzhāo.
The authorities arrested Shànzhāo
and executed him.
The history records this to serve as a warning.
However, judging by the circumstances,
if Shànzhāo had indeed murdered his father,
he certainly would not have left the knife behind to await examination.
It was likely the bandits devised this plan to kill his son.
1. Spring,
first month,
Jǐhài (day),
Prince Ānchéng Xū was promoted to Grand Mentor,
appointed Minister over the Masses,
and granted special honors.
2. Xīnchǒu (day),
the Zhōu sovereign performed the suburban sacrifice at the southern altar.
3. Guǐhài (day),
the Qí sovereign sent the concurrent Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Zhèng Dàhù, on a diplomatic mission.
4. Xú Dù, Duke of Loyal Sufficiency of Xiāngdōng, died.
5. Second month,
Dīngmǎo (day),
the Zhōu sovereign went to Wǔgōng.
6. The Tūjué Mùgān Kèhán turned against Zhōu,
again promising marriage to the Qí people,
and detained Duke Chún of Chén and others for several years without sending them back.
(Chún and others went to fetch the bride; see the sixth year of the Tiānjiā era of Emperor Wén in the previous scroll.)
They destroyed his yurt,
and it did not stop for ten days.
Mùgān grew fearful,
believing it to be a heavenly reprimand,
and immediately prepared the ceremonies and sent his daughter to Zhōu.
Chún and others escorted her back.
Third month,
Guǐmǎo (day),
they arrived at Cháng'ān.
The Zhōu sovereign performed the rite of personally welcoming her.
Jiǎchén (day),
Zhōu issued a general amnesty.
7. Yǐsì (day),
Qí appointed Prince Dōngpíng Yǎn as Grand General,
Prince Nányáng Chuò as Minister over the Masses,
Xú Xiǎnxiù, Pillar of State with Equipped Office, as Minister of Works,
and Prince Guǎngníng Xiàohéng as President of the Imperial Secretariat.
8. Wùwǔ (day),
Yú Jǐn, Duke of Culture of Yān of Zhōu, died.
Jǐn had high merit and lofty position,
yet served his sovereign with increasing reverence.
Whenever he attended court,
his retinue consisted of no more than two or three horsemen.
When the court had major affairs,
they often consulted with Jǐn.
Jǐn was utterly loyal and offered beneficial counsel;
among the meritorious officials, he was especially trusted and favored.
The rituals and treatment he received were grand and respectful,
consistent from beginning to end without interruption.
He taught his sons,
emphasizing quiet retirement,
yet his descendants flourished,
and most achieved prominence and success.
9. Wú Míngchè took advantage of his victory to advance and attack Jiānglíng.
(Taking advantage of the victory at Dùnkǒu.)
The Liáng sovereign moved out and stationed himself at Jìnán to avoid him.
(Liú Zhāo said: More than ten lǐ north of Jiānglíng County is Jìnán City.)
They fought day and night for a hundred days.
The Liáng generals Mǎ Wǔ and Jí Chè attacked Míngchè
and defeated him.
Míngchè retreated to secure Gōng'ān,
and the Liáng sovereign was then able to return.
10. Summer,
fourth month,
Xīnsì (day),
Zhōu appointed Dáxī Wǔ as Grand Mentor,
Yùchí Jiǒng as Grand Guardian,
and Duke Qí Xiàn as Grand Marshal.
11. The Retired Emperor of Qí went to Jìnyáng.
12. Xú Zhīcái, the Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat of Qí, was skilled in medicine.
The Retired Emperor fell ill,
and Zhīcái treated him,
curing him.
The Director of the Central Secretariat, Hé Shìkāi, wishing to be promoted next,
had Zhīcái sent out to serve as Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
(This sets the stage for when the Qí sovereign fell ill and Zhīcái could not be recalled in time.)
(Wǔdài Zhì: Lǔ Commandery was formerly Yǎnzhōu,
governing at Xiáqiū.)
Guǐmǎo (day),
they appointed Hú Chángrén, the Right Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, as Left Vice Director,
and Shìkāi as Right Vice Director.
Chángrén
was the elder brother of the Retired Empress.
13. Gēngxū (day),
the Zhōu sovereign offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Gēngshēn (day),
he went to the Lǐquán Palace.
(The Lǐquán Palace is the old site of the Hàn Gānquán Palace,
located west of Chíyáng County in Féngyì of Hàn.
Later Wèi established Níngyí County here,
and Suí changed it to Lǐquán County.)
14. Rénxū (day),
the Retired Emperor of Qí returned to Yè.
In the autumn of the 15th year,
in the seventh month,
on the Rényín day,
Suí Huángōng Yáng Zhōng of Zhōu died,
and his son Jiān inherited the title.
Jiān served as Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Xiǎo Gōngbó.
According to Zhōu rituals: Gōngbó belonged to the Tiānguān,
with two Zhōngshì,
and two Xiàshì.
Zhèng Xuán noted: Bó,
means chief;
he was in charge of the officials responsible for guarding the royal palace and their administrative orders,
managing their ranks and order,
and overseeing their labor duties.
Later, Zhōu established Left and Right Gōngbó,
who were in charge of the prohibitions of the imperial guard,
each taking turns on duty within the palace,
with Xiǎo Gōngbó assisting them.
Jiān reported this to Zhōng,
and Zhōng said:
"It is difficult to be a daughter-in-law between two mothers-in-law,
you should not go!"
Jiān then declined the position.
The historian, considering Yáng Zhōng to be perceptive,
recorded his death and this incident.
Yáng Jiān first appears here.
On the Bǐngwǔ day of the 16th,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Tàimiào.
On the Wùwǔ day of the 17th,
the Zhōu ruler returned to Cháng'ān.
On the Rénxū day of the 18th,

and Bómóu as Prince of Guìyáng.
In the eighth month,
Qí requested peace with Zhōu,

In the ninth month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
Qí sent Shìzhōng Húsī Wénlüè to reciprocate.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Guǐhài day,
the Zhōu ruler offered sacrifices at the Tàimiào.
On the Gēngwǔ day of the 21st,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Tàimiào.
On the Xīnsì day of the 22nd,
Qí appointed Guǎngníngwáng Xiàohéng as Lù Shàngshūshì,
Zuǒ Púyè Hú Chángrén as Shàngshūlìng,
Yòu Púyè Hé Shìkāi as Zuǒ Púyè,
and Zhōngshū Jiān Táng Yōng as Yòu Púyè.
In the eleventh month,
on the Rénchén day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
Qí sent Jiān Sànqí Chángshì Lǐ Xié as an envoy.
Sàn,
read as sǎndǎn.
Qí,
read as qíjì.
On the Jiǎchén day of the 25th,
the Zhōu ruler went to Qíyáng.
Wǔdài Zhì: Yōng County in Tàiyuán Commandery had the Qíyáng Palace.
Zhōu sent Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Cuī Yàn and others as envoys to Qí.
Shǐxīngwáng Bómào, because Ānchéngwáng Xū monopolized power,
felt deeply resentful,
and repeatedly spoke malicious words.
On the Jiǎyín day,
using an edict from the Grand Empress Dowager, he falsely accused the Emperor,
saying
"he conspired with Liú Shīzhī and Huá Jiǎo."
The word
"yǐ"
indicates
that the Grand Empress Dowager's edict
was actually issued by Xū.
Huá,
read as hùhuà.
"Emperor Wén's insight into his sons,
was comparable to Emperor Yáo;
his intention to pass the throne to his younger brother,
also matched Tàibó.
Now we can reaffirm his past intention,
and honorably establish a virtuous ruler."
Thus, the Emperor was deposed as Prince of Línhǎi,
and Ānchéngwáng was installed to succeed him.
Another order was issued,
demoting Bómào to Marquis of Wēnmá,

Shěn Yuē said: Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established Wēnmá County based on the Wēnmá ship garrison,
which belonged to Jìn'ān Commandery.
Jìn'ān,
was changed to Jiàn'ān by Suí.
Ānchéngwáng sent bandits to ambush him on the road,
and killed him in his carriage.
The Retired Emperor of Qí fell ill,
and sent a courier to summon Xú Zhīcái,
but he had not yet arrived.
On the Xīnwèi day,
the illness became critical,
and he entrusted state affairs to Hé Shìkāi,

He then died in Shìkāi's hands.
The next day,
Zhīcái arrived,
but was sent back to his province.
Back to Yǎnzhōu.
Fù,
read as fúyòu.
Shìkāi kept the death secret for three days without announcing it.
Huángmén Shìláng Féng Zǐcōng asked the reason,
and Shìkāi said:
"The deaths of Shénwǔ and Wénxiāng

Shénwǔ's death,
see scroll 160, first year of Liáng Wǔdì Tàiqīng;
Wénxiāng's death,
see scroll 162, third year of Tàiqīng.
I fear that some among the dukes and princes may have disloyal intentions,
and I intend to summon them all to Liángfēng Hall,
and then discuss the matter with you."
Shìkāi had long been wary of Tàiwèi Lù Shàngshūshì Zhàojùnwáng Ruì and Lǐngjūn Lóu Dìngyuǎn,

"The late Emperor had already passed the throne to the current Emperor,
and the wealth and status of the ministers
are all due to the grace of the current Emperor and his father.
As long as the high-ranking ministers within the court remain unchanged,
the dukes and princes will certainly have no disloyal intentions.
Times are different and circumstances have changed,
how can this be compared to the days of the Hegemonial Court!
Gāo Huān and Gāo Chéng did not immediately usurp Wèi,
but held Wèi's government,
and the monarchs and ministers of Northern Qí all called it the Hegemonial Court.
Cháo,
read as zhíyáo;
the same below.
The matter of the Emperor's passing,
Zhèng Xuán said: Shēng,
means ascend;
xiá,
means gone.
Ascended and gone,
as if he had become an immortal.
If it is long delayed without announcement,
meaning without holding mourning and donning mourning attire.
Shìkāi then announced the death.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
a general amnesty was declared.
On the Wùyín day,
the Retired Empress was honored as Empress Dowager.
Shìzhōng Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Yuán Wényáo,
because Féng Zǐcōng
was the brother-in-law of Empress Dowager Hú,
feared that he would encourage the Empress Dowager to interfere in court politics,
and conspired with Zhàojùnwáng Ruì and Hé Shìkāi,
to send Zǐcōng away as Prefect of Zhèngzhōu.
Shìzǔ was arrogant, extravagant, and licentious,
with heavy corvée duties and taxes,
causing suffering among officials and people.
History says that Wǔchéng was the one who destroyed Qí.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
an edict was issued:
"All artisans and fine craftsmen everywhere,
are to be dismissed.
The elderly and sick among the palace women and official households in Yèxià, Jìnyáng, and Zhōngshān palaces,
are all to be selected and released.
Qí had Yè Palace, Jìnyáng Palace, and Zhōngshān Palace.
Guānkǒu,
refers to the family members of criminals who were confiscated as government slaves.
They are allowed to return."
Yuánzuò,
refers to those who are implicated in crimes,
meaning they are punished because of their relatives' crimes.
In the 29th week, the Lǎo people of Héngléng in Liángzhōu rebelled.
According to the biography of Zhào Wénbiǎo: Héngléng
is a place name,
located in a perilous and fortified area,
spanning several hundred lǐ,
inhabited by the Lǎo people.
After Wénbiǎo pacified the Lǎo,
he established it as Péngzhōu.
Héng
is pronounced with the initials h and the finals ēng.
Lǎo
is pronounced with the initials l and the finals ǎo;
the same applies below.
Zhào Wénbiǎo served as the Chief Clerk of the Liángzhōu Governor's Office.
Cháng
is pronounced with the initials zh and the finals iǎng.
Wénbiǎo said:
"If we attack from all sides,
the Lǎo will have no way out,
and will certainly fight to the death to resist us,
making it difficult to conquer them.
Now, we shall demonstrate both authority and benevolence:
those who commit evil shall be executed,
and those who follow goodness shall be pacified.
Once good and evil are distinguished,
defeating them will be easy."
He then disseminated this intention throughout the army.
At that time, there were assimilated Lǎo people in the army,
many of whom were relatives or acquaintances of the Héngléng Lǎo,
and they reported this truthfully to them.
Those within the borders who had submitted to the central authority were called assimilated Lǎo.
Wénbiǎo's army had already reached their territory.
Among the Lǎo, there were originally two routes,
one level and one perilous.
Several Lǎo chieftains came to see him,
offering to serve as guides.
Wénbiǎo said:
"This route is broad and level,
there is no need for guides.
You, sirs, should go ahead and comfort and instruct your people,
urging them to come and surrender."
He then sent them away.
Wénbiǎo said to his generals:
"The Lǎo chieftains believe we will advance via the broad route,
and will certainly set up ambushes to intercept us.
We should instead take them by surprise."
He then led his troops along the perilous route.
Ascending to a high point to observe,
they indeed found ambushing troops.
Having lost their stratagem,
the Lǎo vied to lead their people in surrender.
Wénbiǎo pacified and comforted them all,
and still levied taxes from them,
with none daring to disobey.
The Zhōu appointed Wénbiǎo as the Chief Clerk of Péngzhōu.
Péngzhōu was originally the territory of Dàngqú in the Hàn dynasty,
occupied by the Lǎo during Lǐ Shì's time.
The Southern Qí established the Guīhuà Commandery,
and the Liáng established Āngù County and Fúyú Commandery.
Later, the Northern Zhōu established Péngzhōu,
named after Péng Mountain.
In the first year of Tàijiàn
(jǐchǒu, 569)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the xīnmǎo day, the first day of the month,
the Zhōu ruler suspended court assemblies due to the mourning for the Qí Shìzǔ,
and sent the Controller of Accounts, Lǐ Lún, to offer condolences and funeral gifts,
and to attend the burial.
2 On the jiǎwǔ day,
Prince Ānchéng ascended the throne as emperor,
changed the era name,
and issued a general amnesty.
He restored the Grand Empress Dowager to Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager to Empress Wén;
he established Lady Liǔ as empress,
and his heir, Shūbǎo, as crown prince;
he enfeoffed the imperial prince Shūlíng as Prince Shǐxīng,
to continue the sacrifices for Prince Zhāoliè.
Emperor Wén had his son Bómào continue the sacrifices for Prince Shǐxīng Zhāoliè.
After the emperor killed Bómào,
he had Shūlíng continue the sacrifices.
On the yǐwèi day,
the emperor paid homage at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the dīngyǒu day,
he appointed the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Shěn Qīn, as Left Vice Director,
and the Minister of Revenue, Wáng Mài, as Right Vice Director.
Mài
was the grandson of Fèn.
3 On the xīnchǒu day,
the emperor performed sacrifices at the southern suburb.
4 On the rényín day,
he enfeoffed the imperial prince Shūyīng as Prince Yùzhāng,
and Shūjiān as Prince Chángshā.
5 On the wùwǔ day,
the emperor offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
6 The Qí Prince Bólíng Wénjiǎn, Jì,
was the younger brother of the same mother as Shìzǔ,
and served as Governor of Dìngzhōu.
He said to someone:
"The succession should come to me next."
Meaning that according to the order of brothers,
he should also become emperor.
Yǔ
is pronounced with the initials n and the finals iù.
Secretly, he had someone go to the province and kill him,
and he was buried with posthumous honors according to ritual.
7 In the second month,
on the yǐhài day,
the emperor plowed the sacred field.
8 On the jiǎshēn day,
the Qí buried Emperor Wǔchéng at Yǒngpíng Tomb,
with the temple name Shìzǔ.
9 On the yǐ
chǒu day,
the Qí transferred Prince Dōngpíng, Yǎn, to be Prince Lángyá.
10 The Qí sent the Palace Attendant, Chìliè Chángchā, on a diplomatic mission to Zhōu.
The Surname Compendium states: Chìliè
is a compound surname,
originating from the western tribes of the Tuòbá.
11 The Qí appointed the Minister of Works, Xú Xiǎnxiù, as Grand Commandant,
and the Director of the Imperial Secretariat of the Bīng Branch, Lóu Dìngyuǎn, as Minister of Works.
Initially,
the Palace Attendant and Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs, Hé Shìkāi,
was favored and intimate with Emperor Shìzǔ,
entering and leaving the imperial bedchamber
without any restrictions or limits.
Consequently, he gained the favor of Empress Hú.
After Emperor Shìzǔ passed away,
the ruler of Qí, because Hé Shìkāi had received the late emperor's entrustment,
deeply relied on and appointed him,
and his power and authority grew even stronger.

Together with Lóu Dìngyuǎn, the Director of the Department of State Affairs Zhào Yànshēn, the Palace Attendant and Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs Yuán Wényáo, the General of the Three Excellencies Táng Yōng, the Commander of the Imperial Guard Qílián Měng, and Gāo Ānàgōng,
(Lǐ Yánshòu said: Qílián,
their ancestors were of the Jī surname,
at the end of the Warring States period,
they fled the chaos and went beyond the frontier,
taking refuge in the Qílián Mountains,
and thus took the mountain as their surname.
The northern people's pronunciation was corrupted,
hence it became Qílián.
The Wei dynasty's official records of clans state: the Qílián clan originated from the western tribes.)
they were known at the time as
the "Eight Nobles."
The Grand Commandant, Prince Rui of Zhàojùn, the Grand Marshal, Prince Rùn of Féngyì, Prince Yánzōng of Āndé, along with Lóu Dìngyuǎn and Yuán Wényáo, all spoke to the ruler of Qí,
requesting that Hé Shìkāi be sent out to a provincial post.
It happened that Empress Dowager Hú was hosting a banquet for the court nobles in the front hall,
and Prince Rui personally presented Hé Shìkāi's crimes and faults, saying:
"Hé Shìkāi was a favorite courtier of the late emperor,
a fox in the city walls and a rat in the ancestral temple,
accepting bribes,
and defiling and disrupting the palace.
We, your subjects, cannot in good conscience remain silent,
and risk death to state this."
The empress dowager said:
"When the late emperor was alive,
why did you, Princes, not speak?
Do you now wish to bully the orphaned and widowed?
Just drink,
and say no more!"
Prince Rui and the others became even more stern in their words and expressions.
The General of the Three Excellencies Ān Tǔgēn said:
"I am originally a merchant from the Western Regions. (Ān Tǔgēn
was originally a man from Ānxī.
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
the Rouran ruler sent an envoy to Jìnyáng,
and Tǔgēn secretly reported the situation of the Rouran.
Gāo Huān therefore made preparations,
and when the Rouran invaded to plunder,
they returned empty-handed.
Later, Gāo Huān made peace and marriage with the Rouran,
establishing a marital alliance,
and Tǔgēn served as the envoy for all of this.
Subsequently, he returned to Gāo Huān,
and from then on was treated with favor.)
Having received such great kindness,
how dare I cherish my life!
If Hé Shìkāi is not sent out,
the court and the country will not be stable."
The empress dowager said:
"We will discuss this another day,
you Princes may disperse for now!"
Prince Rui and the others either threw their caps to the ground,
or brushed their sleeves and stood up.
The next day,
Prince Rui and the others again went to the Yúnlóng Gate,
and ordered Wényáo to enter and present their petition.
After three attempts,
the empress dowager still would not listen.
The Left Chancellor Duàn Sháo sent Hú Chángcàn to convey the empress dowager's words, saying:
"The late emperor's coffin is still in the mourning hall,
matters are too rushed,
I wish for you, Princes, to reconsider!"
Prince Rui and the others then all bowed and expressed their thanks.
Chángcàn returned to report,
and the empress dowager said:
"To complete the family of my sister and her son,
is the strength of my elder brother."
(Chángcàn
was Empress Dowager Hú's elder brother,
hence she spoke thus.)
The matter was dropped.
The empress dowager and the ruler of Qí summoned Hé Shìkāi for questioning,
and he replied:
"Among the various officials,
the late emperor treated me most generously.
Your Majesty has just begun the mourning period,
and the great ministers all have ambitious designs.
If I am sent out now,
it would precisely be cutting off Your Majesty's wings.
You should say to Prince Rui: 'Wényáo and I,
both received appointments from the late emperor.
How can one go and one stay!
Both can be appointed as provincial governors,
and for now, the handling of imperial decrees will remain as before.
The Department of State Affairs issues and receives imperial commands,
let them for now retain their duties as before.
Then send them out.'
Prince Rui and the others will think that I am truly leaving,
and their hearts will surely be pleased."
The emperor and the empress dowager agreed,
and informed Prince Rui and the others as he had said.
Then they appointed Hé Shìkāi as Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
and Wényáo as Governor of Xīyǎnzhōu.
(Xīyǎnzhōu
at that time had its seat at Huátái.)
Prince Rui and the others urged Hé Shìkāi to set off on his journey.
The empress dowager wanted to keep Hé Shìkāi until after the hundred-day mourning period. (In ancient times, the burial day was the yú sacrifice.
After the three yú sacrifices,
the zúkū ceremony was held on a gāng day.
Later generations held the zúkū ceremony after a hundred days,
and this continues to the present.)
Within a few days,
the empress dowager repeatedly brought this up.
A palace attendant who knew the empress dowager's secret intent
said to Prince Rui:
"Since the empress dowager's mind is set thus,
why must Your Highness insist on opposing it!"
Prince Rui said:
"I have received a weighty commission.
Now the successor ruler is young and immature,
how can we allow treacherous ministers at his side!
If I do not guard against this even unto death,
what face have I to look upon heaven!"
He then went again to see the empress dowager,
and earnestly argued his case.
The empress dowager ordered wine to be poured and presented to Prince Rui,
but Prince Rui said sternly:
"Today we are discussing matters of great importance to the state,
not for a cup of wine!"
Having spoken,
he abruptly left.
Hé Shìkāi, carrying beautiful women and a pearl curtain, went to see Lóu Dìngyuǎn,
and said in gratitude:
"The various nobles wished to kill me,
but thanks to Your Highness's efforts,
(Emperor Wǔchéng had enfeoffed Lóu Dìngyuǎn as Prince of Línhuái Commandery,
hence he addressed him thus.)
I have been appointed as a provincial governor.
Now that I am about to take my leave,
I respectfully present two women
and one pearl curtain."
Dìngyuǎn was pleased,
and said to Hé Shìkāi:
"Do you wish to return to the capital?"
Hé Shìkāi said:
"Having been inside for so long, I have long felt uneasy.
Now that I can leave,
it truly fulfills my original wish.
I do not wish to enter again.
I only beg Your Highness for protection,
to long remain as a great provincial governor is enough."
Dìngyuǎn believed him.
As he escorted him to the gate,
Hé Shìkāi said:
"Now that I am going far away,
I wish to bid farewell and pay my respects to the two palaces."
Dìngyuǎn permitted it.
Hé Shìkāi thus was able to see the empress dowager and the emperor,
and presented his argument, saying:
"Once the late emperor ascended to the distant heavens,
I was ashamed that I could not follow him in death.
Observing the intentions and momentum of the court nobles,
they wish to make Your Majesty into another Qiánmíng.
(Qiánmíng
was the era name of the Prince of Jìnán of Qí.
The events are recorded in the 168th scroll, the first year of the Tiānjiā era of Emperor Wén of Chén.)
There will certainly be a great upheaval.
What face have I to see the late emperor beneath the earth!"
Thereupon he wailed bitterly.
The emperor and empress dowager both wept,
and asked:
"What plan is there?"
Hé Shìkāi said:
"I have already been able to enter,
what further worries are there?
We only need a few lines of an imperial edict."
Thereupon an edict was issued sending Dìngyuǎn out as Governor of Qīngzhōu,
and reprimanding Prince Rui of Zhàojùn for the crime of disloyalty.
The next day,
Ruì was about to enter again to remonstrate,
but his wife and children all stopped him.
Ruì said,
"The affairs of the state are of great importance.
I would rather die serving the late emperor
than endure witnessing the court's ruin."
When he reached the gates of the palace,
someone else told him:
"Your Highness, do not enter,
I'm afraid there might be trouble."
Ruì replied:
"I have not failed Heaven;
to die would bring no regret."
He entered,
and saw the Empress Dowager,
who again spoke on the matter,
but Ruì stood even more firmly.
As he left,
when he reached Yong Lane,
he encountered soldiers
who captured and sent him to Huálín Park's Que Lí Buddha Temple.
Records of the Western Regions by the Monk Xuánzàng: Forty li north of the State of Qiūcí,
there is a temple on the mountain
called Que Lí,
which is very serene,
so it was imitated in the construction of the Buddhist temple.
Ruì had long managed state affairs.
During the time of Emperor Wénxuān,
Jǐnán acted as the regent,
establishing the Grand Commandant's Office,
jointly overseeing public affairs with the Department of State Affairs,
and Ruì served as the chief historical officer of the Grand Commandant's Office.
During the era of Wǔchéng,
he was appointed as Minister of State Affairs,
then advanced to director of state affairs,
and further to Grand Commandant.
The court,
with Zhíyáo Fān;
similarly below.
The court and the populace mourned his loss.
Once again entrusted Shìkāi with the position of Palace Secretary and Left Guard Captain.
Dìngyuǎn returned the gifts from Shìkāi,
adding additional treasures to bribe him.
In the third month,
the ruler of Qí went to Jìnyáng.
In the summer,
in April,
on the Day of Jiǎzǐ,
the Shàngshū Department of Bìng Province became the Great Jīngshèng Temple,
and the Jìn Temple became the Great Chónghuáng Temple.
Wèi Shōu's Records: In Jìnyáng County, Tài Yuán Commandery, there is the Jìn Temple.
On the Day of Yǐchǒu,
the ruler of Qí returned to Yè.
The young ruler of Qí,
had many favorites.
General of the Martial Guards Gāo Ānà Gōng,
who was always favored by the Emperor and Shìkāi for his flattery,
was often ordered by the Emperor to attend the ruler of Qí in the Eastern Palace,
thus gaining favor;
he repeatedly rose to the position of Shàngshū Director of the Departments,
and was conferred the title of Prince of Huáiyīn.
The late Emperor selected twenty supervisors,
to guard the Eastern Palace,
the Left and Right Guard Houses led the Left and Right Houses,
each department's regular and deputy supervisors,
each had a chief and vice chief supervising them.
The ruler of Qí solely favored Zhǎng Luán.
Zhǎng Luán,
whose given name was Fèng,
went by his courtesy name,
rose repeatedly to the position of Palace Secretary and Commander of Military Affairs,
managing the secrets within the institution.
Palace maid Lù Lìngxuān,
whose husband was Luò Chāo of Hànhuáng,
was executed for plotting rebellion,
Lìngxuān was sent to the women's courtyard,
her son, Tíbā,
was also enslaved.
When the ruler of Qí was an infant,
Lìngxuān nurtured him.
Lìngxuān was clever and cunning,
skilled at pleasing others,
she was favored by Princess Hú,
and within the palace,
she wielded significant power,
and was granted the title of Lady of the County.
Both Shìkāi and Gāo Ānà Gōng treated her as their adoptive mother.
The ruler of Qí appointed Lìngxuān as Female Palace Secretary.
After Emperor Wén of the Later Wèi dynasty reformed the inner officials,
in addition to the Left and Right Companions, Three Consorts, Nine Ladies, Attendants, and Court Girls,
he established the Inner Positions,
overseeing the Inner Bureau,
comparable to the Ministers of State Affairs and Treasurer;
creating positions of Supervisor, Senior Overseer, and Female Palace Secretary,
equivalent to Director of the Second Rank.
They played and laughed frivolously day and night,
rising repeatedly to become Grand Prefect with Three Tribunes, Grand General of the Martial Guards.
Palace person Mù Shèlì,
a maidservant of Húlǜ Empress,
was favored by the ruler of Qí;
Lìngxuān sought to associate with her,
thus becoming her foster mother,
recommending her as Lady of Great Virtue.
The new decree of Héqīng: the three consorts of Grand Virtue, High Virtue, and Righteous Virtue,
held ranks equivalent to the Three Ministers.
However, Shìkāi was the longest in power,
all favored ministers relied on him to secure their favor.
The ruler of Qí remembered Zǔ Tǐng;
the ruler of Qí received abdication,
Zǔ Tǐng initiated the plan,
hence remembered him.
Zǔ Tǐng was relocated to Guāng Prefecture last year.
The Five Dynasties Records: Dōnghǎi Commandery,
Liáng established South and North two Qīng Prefectures,
Dōngwèi changed it to Hǎi Prefecture.
"Zhào Yànshēn is deeply conniving,
seeking to imitate the actions of Yī and Huò,
how can those like Yí Tóng and Jiě Dì remain safe,
why not employ wise men early! "
Shìkāi also considered Tǐng daring and resourceful,
wanted to bring him as a chief strategist,
thus abandoning old grievances,
treating him with genuine respect,
and spoke with the lady of Lù to the Emperor:
"The sons of Xiāng, Xuān, and Zhāo three emperors,
all failed to ascend.
Referring to the sons of Wénxiāng, Wénxuān, and Xiàozhāo.
It was due to the efforts of Zǔ Xiàozhēng.
Zǔ Tǐng,
courtesy name Xiàozhēng,
whose affairs are recorded in the previous scroll, Emperor Wén's Tiānjiā first year.
His services cannot go unrewarded.
Although Xiàozhēng's conduct is lacking,
his extraordinary strategy surpasses others,
he could be used in times of crisis.
Moreover, the man is already blind,
surely he harbors no disloyalty,
please summon him,
to advise on planning."
The ruler of Qí agreed,
summoned him,
appointed him Director of the Library,
and promoted him to Grand Prefect with Three Tribunes.
Shìkāi slandered Minister of State Affairs, Lǒngdōng Prince Hú Chángrén, as arrogant and willful,
exiling him as Governor of Qí Prefecture.
Chángrén was angered and resentful,
scheming to send assassins to kill Shìkāi.
When the plot was discovered,
Shìkāi and Tǐng planned in response,
Tǐng cited the precedent of Emperor Wén of Hàn executing Bó Zhāo,
the matter of Bó Zhāo is recorded in the fourteenth scroll, the tenth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn.
Hú Chángrén,
was the Emperor's uncle,
hence citing this to execute him.
In May,
on the Day of Gēngxū,
the Lord of Zhōu went to Lǐquán Palace.
On the Day of Dīngsì,
Xú Líng, Minister of the Department of Personnel, was appointed Left Guard Captain.
In autumn,
in July,
on the Day of Xīnmǎo,
the Crown Prince took a wife from the Shěn clan,
examine discrepancies: Chénshū, Southern History records the biography of Shěn Empress,
stating the Crown Prince was granted the title in the third year of Taijiàn,
which is incorrect.
Now, we follow the Imperial Annals.
On the Day of Xīnhài,
the Lord of Zhōu returned to Cháng’ān.
In August,
on the Day of Gēngchén,
bandits killed the commander of Zhōu's Kongchéng defense,
and the land was taken by Qí.
Wèi Shōu's Records: In Hàn and Jìn's Hénán Xīnchéng County,
Later Wèi established Xīnchéng Commandery,
governing at Kongchéng.
The land was within the territory of Suí's Hénán Commandery, Yīquē County.
In September,
on the Day of Xīnmǎo,
Zhōu dispatched Duke Xiàn of Qí and Commander Lǐ Mù to lead troops to Yíyáng,
Dù Yòu says: Yíyáng Commandery,
now Fúchāng County.
Ōuyáng Hē had been stationed in Guǎngzhōu for more than ten years,
in the second year of Emperor Wǔ's Yǒngdìng,
Hē and his father Wěi established peace in Guǎngzhōu,
by then, it had been twelve years in total.
Hē,
pronounced as Xiàbù.
Since Huá Jiǎo's rebellion,
the Emperor was suspicious of him,
so he was summoned as Left Guard General.
Hē was fearful,
and many of his subordinates urged him to rebel,
so he raised an army and attacked Qián Dàojí, Commissioner of Héngzhōu.
This refers to the Héngzhōu of Shǐxīng.
The Five Dynasties Records: Nánhǎi Commandery, Shǐxīng County,
Liáng established Ānyuǎn Commandery and Eastern Héngzhōu.
The emperor dispatched the Secretariat Director Xú Jiǎn to deliver an edict with credentials.
When Ōu Yāngé first saw Jiǎn,
he displayed a grand array of guards and ceremonial regalia,
and his words were disrespectful.
Jiǎn said:
"The affair of Lǚ Jiā
is indeed far in the past,
(The affair of Lǚ Jiā is recorded in the 20th scroll, in the fifth and sixth years of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.)
Zhōu Dí and Chén Bǎoyìng both rebelled and were defeated and died,
(These events are also recorded in the Annals of Emperor Wén.)
but it is not too late for you."
Yāngé fell silent and did not respond,
then placed Jiǎn in the Gūyuán Temple,
where he was detained for several decades without being allowed to return.
Yāngé once went out to see Jiǎn,
and Jiǎn said to him:
"General, you have already raised your banner in revolt.
I, Jiǎn, must return to report to the Son of Heaven.
My life
is in your hands, General,
but your success or failure
does not depend on me.
I hope you will not detain me."
Yāngé then sent Jiǎn back.
Jiǎn
was the son of Xú Líng.
(Xú Líng was then a high-ranking and prominent official in the Chén court.)
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
an edict ordered the General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhāng Zhāodá to attack Yāngé.
On the Rénwǔ day,
the emperor offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Zhōu's Duke of Zēngwén, Chángsūn Jiǎn, died.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
Qí appointed Húlǜ Guāng as Grand Tutor,
Féngyì King Rùn as Grand Guardian,
and Lángyá King Yǎn as Grand Marshal.
In the twelfth month,
on the Gēngwǔ day,
Lánlíng King Chánggōng was appointed as President of the Imperial Secretariat.
On the Gēngchén day,
Wèi Shōu, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was appointed as Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Zhōu's Duke of Qí, Yǔwén Xiàn, and others besieged Qí's Yíyáng,
cutting off its supply routes.
Since the rebellion of Huá Jiǎo,
relations with the people of Zhōu had been severed.
At this time, Zhōu sent the Grand Master of the Imperial Secretariat Dù Gǎo on a diplomatic mission,
requesting the restoration of former friendly relations.
(Dù Gǎo had been sent on diplomatic missions to Chén many times, hence he was sent to restore former friendly relations.)
(Fù, read as fù yòu fān.)
(Hǎo, read as hū dào fān.)
An envoy was sent to Zhōu.
In spring,
the first month,
on the Yǐyǒu day, the first day of the month,
Qí changed its era name to Wǔpíng.
Qí's King of Dōng'ān, Lóu Ruì, died.
(He was the Prince of Dōng'ān Commandery.)
(Wǔdài Zhì: Yíshuǐ County in Lángyá Commandery was formerly the seat of Dōng'ān Commandery.)
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
the emperor offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the Wùshēn day,
Qí sent the concurrent Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Péi Yànzhī on a diplomatic mission.
(Sàn, read as sì dǎn fān.)
(Qí, read as qí jì fān.)
(Yàn, read as yú jiǎn fān, also yú liè fān.)
Qí's Grand Tutor Húlǜ Guāng,
leading thirty thousand infantry and cavalry, went to rescue Yíyáng.
He repeatedly defeated the Zhōu army,
built the Tǒngguān and Fēnghuà fortifications,
and then returned.
The Zhōu army pursued him,
but Guāng launched a counterattack,
again defeating them,
and captured their Kaifu Yitong Sansi Yǔwén Yīng and Liáng Jǐngxīng.
Although the Zhōu army was repeatedly defeated,
they did not cease their attack on Yíyáng.
On the Jǐsì day,
Qí appointed Húlǜ Guāng as Right Counselor-in-Chief and Governor of Bìng Province,
and also appointed Rènchéng King Jiē as Grand Preceptor,
and Hèbá Rén as Recorder of Imperial Secretariat Affairs.
Ōu Yāngé summoned the Administrator of Yángchūn, Féng Pú, to Nánhǎi.
(Wǔdài Zhì: Yángchūn County in Gāoliáng Commandery; Liáng established Yángchūn Commandery there. Guǎngzhōu's seat was in Nánhǎi Commandery.)
(Shǒu, read as shì yòu fān.)
Pú sent an envoy to inform his mother, Xiǎn Fūrén.
The lady said:
"I have been loyal and steadfast
for two generations now."
(Pú and his father Róng represent the two generations.)
(Yòu, read as yǒu.)
(Shǐ, read as shū lì fān.)
(Xiǎn, read as xī diǎn fān.)
She then raised troops to guard the border,
and led the various tribal chiefs to welcome Zhāng Zhāodá.
Zhāodá advanced with double speed,
and reached Shǐxīng.
When Yāngé heard that Zhāodá had suddenly arrived,

He thus adopted the old laws of the Wei and Jin dynasties,
extending down to those of the Qi and Liang dynasties,

(What was followed across generations is called continuity;
what underwent alterations is called change.)

Whenever there were doubts or ambiguities,

Consequently, the previous practices of displaying severed heads, dismemberment by chariot, and flogging were abolished.
(Displaying severed heads involved beheading and hanging the head on a wooden pole.
Dismemberment by chariot involved tearing the body apart with chariots in the marketplace.
The Liang system had regulated flogging, legal flogging, and ordinary flogging,
with three grades of distinction.
Regulated flogging used raw leather with the edges trimmed;
legal flogging used raw leather without trimming the edges;
ordinary flogging used tanned leather without trimming the edges;
all were shaped like a crane’s head.
The handle was one foot and one inch long,
the tip was two feet and seven inches long,
the width was three inches,

The Emperor extensively built palaces and halls,
indulging his senses to the extreme,
depleting the treasury,
and whenever there were construction projects,
he was constantly troubled by insufficient funds.
Kèqīng memorialized requesting that taxes on markets and trade be levied regardless of whether the people were scholars or commoners,
and furthermore, to increase them beyond the old rates.
Consequently, Yáng Huìlǎng was appointed as Grand Market Director,
and Jì Huìjǐng as Chief Clerk of the Ministry of Revenue and Granaries.
(Under the Liáng system: the Grand Market Director was subordinate to the Minister of the Imperial Treasury,
with a rank of six hundred shi).
(The Chief Clerk of the Ministry of Revenue and Granaries
refers to the Chief Clerk of the Revenue and Granary Sections).
(Under the Liáng system,
the Chief Clerk of the Secretariat was equivalent in status to a Court Gentleman Consultant).
(Héng,
pronounced hù dēng).
They examined and checked the account books,
with not the slightest discrepancy;
however, they all failed to grasp the broader principles,
supervising and demanding with harsh and petty scrutiny,
amassing wealth without satiation,
causing scholars and commoners alike to lament and resent them.
Kèqīng oversaw them overall,
and the annual revenue collected
exceeded the usual amounts by several tens of times.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and even more so considered Shī Wénqìng a good judge of character.
(A ruler on the brink of chaos
each deems his ministers worthy,
this indeed holds true).
All matters, great and small,
were entrusted to them without exception;
they recommended and promoted one another in turn,
(just as those drawing water pull the rope expecting it to rise,
ministers recommending each other
is also like this).
Kǒng Fàn considered himself talented in both civil and military affairs,

"The various generals outside the court,
having risen from the ranks,
are merely a match for ordinary men.
Profound insight and far-sighted planning,
how could they possibly understand!"
The Emperor asked Shī Wénqìng about this,
and Wénqìng, fearing Fàn,
also agreed;
Sīmǎ Shēn further endorsed it.
From then on, whenever a general or commander had even a minor fault,
their troops were immediately taken away,

Rèn Zhōng’s troops were taken and assigned to Fàn and Cài Zhēng.
As a result, civil and military officials became disunited,
leading to the dynasty’s collapse.
(The *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* details the reasons for the Chén dynasty’s fall).
