arriving at dawn
and attacking;
Xīn was defeated and fled,
his entire force captured.
Sù rewarded and sent them away,
without the slightest violation.
Sù led the naval forces eastward,
vessels covering the river,
banners and armor gleaming in the sun.
Sù sat on a large command ship,
his appearance majestic and imposing.
The Chén people who saw him
were all terrified,
saying:
"The Duke of Qīnghé is the river god!"
The garrisons along the river heard that the Sui army was about to arrive,
and they reported it one after another;
however, Shī Wénqìng and Shěn Kèqīng both suppressed the reports and did not inform the emperor.
Earlier,
the emperor, because Xiāo Yán and Xiāo Huán,
members of the Liang imperial clan,
had come over with their troops,
was inwardly wary of them.
Therefore, he dispersed their forces to distant places,
appointing Yán as the governor of Dōngyáng Prefecture,
and Huán as the governor of Wú Prefecture.
He sent Rèn Zhōng, the commander of the army, to guard Wúxīng Commandery,
to serve as a strategic link between the two prefectures.
He appointed Prince Nánpíng, Yí, to guard Jiāng Prefecture,
and Prince Yǒngjiā, Yàn, to guard Nánxú Prefecture.
The seat of Jiāng Prefecture was Xúnyáng,
and the seat of Nánxú Prefecture was Jīngkǒu,
both being important strongholds along the river.
Yí,
yú lì fān.
He ordered all defensive ships along the river to follow the two princes back to the capital,
to display military might and intimidate those who had come from Liáng.
As a result, there was not a single warship on the river,
and the troops from the upper reaches were all blocked by Yáng Sù's army,
unable to arrive.
Prince Jìnxi of Xiāng Prefecture, Shūwén,
the seat of Xiāng Prefecture was Chángshā.
enjoyed great popularity among the people.
The emperor, because he controlled the upper reaches,
secretly distrusted him.
Considering that he had shown little favor to his ministers in the past,
he feared they would not be of use,
and there was no one suitable to appoint.
Therefore, he promoted Shī Wénqìng to the positions of military governor and governor of Xiāng Prefecture,
assigning him two thousand elite troops,
intending to send him westward;
meanwhile, he recalled Shūwén to the court.
Wénqìng was greatly pleased with this matter,
but he feared that after going out,
those in charge would find fault with him,
so he recommended his associate Shěn Kèqīng to replace him.
Before they departed,
the two of them jointly handled confidential matters.
General Hùjūn, Fán Yì, said to Vice Director Yuán Xiàn:
"Jīngkǒu and Cǎishí are both crucial locations,
each requiring five thousand elite troops,
along with two hundred 'golden-winged' ships,
to patrol up and down the river,
as a defensive measure."
Golden-winged,
the name of a ship.
Then, together with the civil and military ministers,
they requested to implement Yì's strategy.
Not long after,
Hán Qínhǔ crossed at Cǎishí,
and Hè Ruòbì captured Jīngkǒu,
the two armies advanced simultaneously,
and Chén perished.
There are places that must be defended,
a fact that even those without great wisdom can understand.
Abolishing their duty to report,
Mèngzǐ said: "When feudal lords come to court to see the Son of Heaven, it is called 'shùzhí' (reporting on duties)."
Here, going out to guard the frontiers is considered 'shùzhí'.
Zhī,
means to go.
Rèn,
means duty.
Zhī rèn,
means going to assume one's duty.
Wénqìng and Kèqīng at that time jointly handled confidential matters.
If Wénqìng went out,
then Kèqīng would have sole control.
"If there must be discussions,
there is no need to present them in person;
simply write a memorial,
and it will be submitted."
This means that if court officials must present something,
they do not need to see the Chén ruler in person to say it;
as long as it is in writing,
it will be conveyed.
Wéi,
yú wèi fān;
xià nèi wéi tóng.
The two men brought the memorial in to report.
The emperor said:
"This is a routine matter,
the border city commanders are sufficient to handle it.
If we deploy troops and ships,
it will surely cause alarm and disturbance."
When the Sui army reached the river,
spies arrived urgently,
and Xiàn and others earnestly petitioned,
repeatedly.
Wénqìng said:
"The New Year's assembly is approaching,
and on the day of the southern suburb sacrifice,
the crown prince will have many attendants;
Chén followed the Liáng system,
performing the sacrifice to heaven and earth at the southern and northern suburbs on the first xīn day of the first month in alternate years,
using a special ox.
It seems that this ritual was to be performed in the coming first month,
hence Shī Wénqìng spoke thus.
Cóng,
cái yòng fān.
Matters will be neglected."
The emperor said:
"Now we will send out troops,
and if the northern border is peaceful,
we can use the navy to accompany the suburban sacrifice,
why would that not be possible!"
He also said:
"If we do this, neighboring states will hear of it,
and they will think our country is weak."
Later, he also used bribes to influence Jiǎng Zǒng,
and Zǒng internally lobbied for him,
meaning that after various opinions were presented,
Wénqìng again used bribes to influence Jiǎng Zǒng,
to make him assist himself.
Shuō,
shū ruì fān.
Zhòng,
rú zì.
Then he ordered the matter to be submitted for detailed discussion.
Zǒng also suppressed Xiàn and others,
so the discussion dragged on without resolution.
The emperor calmly said to his attendants:
"The royal aura is here.
The Qí army came three times,
the Zhōu army came twice,
and each time they were crushed and defeated.
The Qí army came three times,
refers to the first year of Shàotài of Liáng Emperor Jìng, when Xú Sìhuī and Rèn Yuē led the Qí army to attack Jiànkāng,
occupying Shítóu.
In the first year of Tàipíng,
they again attacked and captured Cǎishí,
and together with Qí's Xiāo Guǐ invaded,
threatening Jiànkāng.
In the first year of Tiānjiā of Emperor Shìzǔ,
Qí generals Liú Bóqiú and Mùróng Shìdé assisted Wáng Lín in capturing Wúhú,
but they were all defeated.
The Zhōu army came twice,
refers to the first year of Tiānjiā when Dúgū Shèng and Hè Ruòdūn entered Xiāngchuān,
and in the first year of Guāngdà of Prince Línhǎi,
Yǔwén Zhí and Yuán Dìng assisted Huá Jiǎo,
and they were all defeated.
Cóng,
qiān róng fān.
The Minister of Personnel, Kǒng Fàn, said:
"The Yangtze River is a natural moat,
since ancient times it has served as a boundary separating north and south.
When Emperor Wén of Wèi attacked Wú,
he reached the river,
saw the surging waves,
and sighed:
'Truly, heaven has set this as the boundary between north and south.'
Qiàn,
qī yàn fān.
The border generals want to achieve merit,
so they falsely claim the situation is urgent.
I have often regretted that my official rank is low;
if the enemy crosses the river,
I will surely become the Duke of Tàiwèi!"
Kǒng Fàn considered himself both civil and military,
hence he boasted grandly to pretend he would achieve merit.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
it has been customary to refer to the three dukes as Duke Tàiwèi, Duke Sītú, and Duke Sīkōng.
Fàn said:
"These are our horses,
why should they die!"
Meaning that if the horses cross the river,
they will certainly not be able to return north,
and will all become ours—
also a grand boast.
Therefore, they did not make thorough preparations,
but continued to perform music, indulge in drinking, and compose poetry without cease.
In this year,
the Tǔyùhún subordinate king Tuòbá Mùmí
(The Tǔyùhún also had the surname Tuòbá.)
Subordinate,
pronounced bēi.
Tǔ,
pronounced with the entering tone from tūn.
Yù,
pronounced yù.
The Suí sovereign said:
"Under the vast heavens,
all are my subjects.
In my nurturing and care,
I uphold benevolence and filial piety.
The deluded and frenzied Hún bandits,
with their wives and children filled with terror,
all wish to submit and reform,
to save themselves from peril and destruction.
However, those who betray their husbands and turn against their fathers
cannot be accepted.
Moreover, their original intent was precisely to avoid death.
Now, if I reject them,
it would again be lacking in benevolence.
If further news arrives,
you should only comfort and pacify them,
allowing them to come of their own accord,
without needing to dispatch troops to receive them.
As for their brothers-in-law and nephews who wish to come,
also allow them to follow their own wishes,
without troubling to persuade or entice them."
The so-called
"betray their husbands and turn against their fathers"
"brothers-in-law and nephews",
must have all referred to specific individuals at the time,
but the historical records do not provide detailed accounts.
The Suí Shū writes
"the famous king Tuòbá Mùmí",
"subordinate king"
also uses the terminology from the Hàn Shū.
Bèi (turn against),
pronounced with the tone from pú mèi.
Yòu (entice),
pronounced with the tone from yáng jiǔ.
11. The King of Hénán, Yízī Póu, died.
The Suí sovereign ordered his younger brother, Shùguī, to succeed him and command his people.
(Yízī Póu's surrender to Suí is recorded in the previous volume, the thirteenth year of Gāozōng's Tàijiàn era.)
Póu,
pronounced with the tone from pú hóu.
Zú (died),
pronounced with the tone from zǐ xù.
